messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

It was a year and a half ago that the story ended, but for David, the film never stops. A 45-year-old journalist, he had been embedded with a local militia in a conflict zone, reporting on a ceasefire that never held. He was taken by a rival faction and held for eleven days in a concrete room, beaten, and repeatedly threatened with execution. The smell of cheap alcohol on his captors’ breath was the constant, nauseating backdrop; the pain in his neck from the zip-ties and the rough handling was a dull, permanent anchor to each moment of terror. When he was finally released in a prisoner exchange, he told himself he was fine. He went home to his wife, returned to his desk, and tried to file the story. But the story was filing him.

The memory does not wait for permission. It arrives as a complete, sensory film—the scrape of the chair, the pressure of the blindfold, the smell of alcohol, the terror that was so absolute it felt like dying. And because remembering brings back that same raw terror, his body reacts as if the event is happening again, right now. This is why a sudden sound—a car backfiring, a dropped pan in the kitchen—will send him diving for cover, his heart hammering, his neck seizing with the old familiar pain. He has come to believe that he is permanently broken, that any unexpected noise is a potential threat, that he must be superalert or he will be caught off guard. This hypervigilance has become his default state, a constant scanning for danger that leaves him exhausted and irritable.

The most insidious loop, however, involves his wife. A simple, loving touch on the shoulder from behind can trigger the same physical startle response as a guard’s hand grabbing his collar. The neck pain, which he now associates directly with the captivity, flares up whenever he is tense, and he finds himself bracing for a blow during a hug. He has begun to pull away from her, not because he does not love her, but because the sensation of being touched has become so tightly wired to the memory of being handled roughly that he cannot separate the two. His hypervigilance means he is constantly monitoring for the next sound, the next touch, the next smell—and that constant state of alert primes his memory to replay the worst moments, creating a cycle that tightens with every passing week.

He now avoids the corner of the grocery store where the cleaning alcohol is kept. He has stopped meeting colleagues for drinks, because the smell of whiskey on someone’s breath at a bar is enough to make him nauseous and dissociate for a full minute. At work, he has shifted from field reporting to desk editing, a move that has quietly stalled his career. His editor has noticed the drop in initiative; David cannot explain that he is too busy watching the door. What finally brought him to seek help was not the flashbacks or the startle responses—he had learned to live with those. It was the moment last week when his wife, reaching out to comfort him after a nightmare, saw him flinch and pull away, and her face crumpled with a hurt he could not bear to see again. He is terrified that the man who survived the room is destroying the life he came home to.
